title: is doubt okay?
hookLine: the question people type late at night: is it haram to doubt?
carry: ask, so the heart can rest

cards: It's late, the phone is the only light in the room, and someone types a question they'd never ask out loud: is it haram to doubt your faith? A question from a class that won't go away. A stretch when prayer felt empty.
Underneath it is one worry: if I have questions, am I still in? Before any rule, this path starts there, because the oldest answers are gentler than people expect.

teach.h: IMAN — FROM A ROOT OF SAFETY AND TRUST.
teach.b: Start with the word for faith: iman. Its root, a-m-n, is the root of safety and of trust; the same root gives amana, something entrusted to you. So iman is less a certificate you hold and more a trust you live in.

The Qur'an even speaks of believers adding faith to their faith, as if it can grow. That's why people say my iman is low when prayer goes dry for a while: a faith that can grow can also dip, and come back.
Now the question. Some of the Prophet Muhammad's ﷺ companions once came to him, troubled. We find thoughts in ourselves, they said, so bad we can hardly bring ourselves to say them.
Do you really find that? he asked. Yes.
That, he said, is clear faith. Not the thought itself: being troubled by it. Their discomfort showed how much they cared.
And the Qur'an tells of a prophet who asked. Ibrahim, Abraham, says: my Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. Don't you believe? comes the reply.

teach.h: SHOW ME, SO MY HEART MAY BE AT EASE.
teach.b: And he answers: “Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease.” He isn't scolded. He's shown.
Scholars have a lot to say about the difference between a passing question and turning away, and this path will get there.
For today, the plain part: in these stories, asking is a way of looking for rest.
And if a late-night question ever comes with real darkness, the kind where you can't see a way through, please reach out tonight: 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

how: Muslims speak of iman, faith, as something that grows and weakens over a life; many bring their questions to a teacher, an imam or a study circle, and the Qur'an and hadith are often read for answers to doubt.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: faith, from a root of safety and trust
the Prophet's answer to his troubled companions
asked to see, so his heart could rest

s: having a troubling thought means your faith is gone
a saying of the Prophet ﷺ calls being troubled by such thoughts clear faith.
in the Qur'an, a prophet asks God to show him
Ibrahim asks to see how God gives life to the dead, so that his heart may be at ease.
the Qur'an speaks of faith that can grow
it speaks of believers adding faith to their faith.

games.q: some of the companions come to the Prophet ﷺ, ashamed of thoughts they can hardly say out loud. what does he tell them?
games.why: that is clear faith: not the thought, but being troubled by it. he met their shame with reassurance.

p: yes, so my heart can rest

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, let one honest question come up, whatever it is. On the second, don't answer it; just hold it, the way Ibrahim held his.
On the third, breathe out, and let your heart rest a moment, with the question still open.

wordCard.voice: Iman. Faith: from a root of safety and trust, a faith that can grow, with room for questions. Fifth word.

orig.note: Arabic: faith, from the root a-m-n, safety and trust. amana (a trust) and al-Amin (the trustworthy) share it.

carryVoice: Your line: ask, so the heart can rest. Ibrahim asked, and he wasn't turned away. Day five, done.

sources.q: Yea, but (I ask) in order that my heart may be at ease.

sources.ref: Qur'an 48:4 (that they might add faith unto their faith)
Sahih Muslim 132 (the companions' troubling thoughts: 'that is clear faith')
